guides.title: What to Eat When Nothing Sounds Good
guides.subtitle: Gentle, small, mostly no-cook ideas for low-appetite days, and a few habits that make eating a little easier.
intro: Some days, food just does not sound good. Maybe your appetite is smaller than it used to be, maybe smells feel stronger, or maybe you are simply tired. On those days, the goal is not a perfect meal. It is getting something useful in, in a form that feels manageable.

This guide collects the foods and habits we lean on when appetite is low: cooler temperatures, milder flavors, softer textures and portions small enough to finish. It is general cooking education, not medical advice. If eating or drinking feels hard, or you are worried about how you feel, talk to your care team.
takeaways: Smaller portions, more often, can feel easier than three full meals.
Cool or warm food usually smells less than hot food.
Start with the protein while your appetite is at its best.
Keep a few no-cook options ready so a hard day needs no cooking.

p: A full plate can feel like a wall on a low-appetite day. Serve half of what you think you can eat, finish it, and go back only if you want to. A half bowl you finish counts for more than a full one you push away.
list: Use smaller plates and bowls: A dessert plate or a mug makes a small portion look less daunting.
Eat at regular times: Small meals every few hours can be easier than waiting until you feel hungry.
Sip between meals: Drinking a lot with a meal can make you feel full sooner, so many people sip between meals instead.

p: Temperature and texture make a big difference. Hot food releases more aroma, which can be off-putting when your stomach feels unsettled. Cool or lukewarm food, mild seasoning and soft textures are often easier to face.

head: Instead of
Try
rows: Soup served warm, sipped from a mug
The same dish with sweet paprika and less garlic
Soft eggs, yogurt, blended soups, flaky fish
A small bowl with more protein than pasta
Salmon served at room temperature, or canned tuna

sections.h: No-Cook Options to Keep on Hand
p: On the hardest days, cooking is the barrier. Keep a few of these in the fridge or pantry so there is always something ready. Protein amounts are estimates; check labels.
list: Plain Greek yogurt: About 17 g protein in a 3/4-cup serving. Add berries or a little honey.
Cottage cheese: About 12 g protein in 1/2 cup. Good with fruit or on a cracker.
Hard-boiled eggs: About 6 g protein each. Make a batch and keep them peeled.
Overnight oats: Cold, soft and already portioned in small jars.
Milk or soy milk: About 7 to 8 g protein per cup, easy to sip slowly.
String cheese and crackers: Small, mild and easy to carry.

p: Each of these recipes has a "Make it gentler" variation, with milder seasoning or a cooler way to serve it.
list: Tomato Basil Soup with White Beans: Smooth, mild and easy to sip from a mug.
Blueberry Vanilla Overnight Oats: Cold, soft and made the night before.
Butternut Squash Soup with White Beans: Gently sweet and velvety.
Lemon Chicken Orzo Soup: Brothy and light. Start with a mug of the broth.

p: Low appetite is common, but some signs mean it is time to call your doctor or care team rather than adjust your menu.
list: You are having trouble keeping food or fluids down.
You feel dizzy or very weak, or notice signs of dehydration such as very dark urine.
You have severe or persistent stomach pain.
You are eating much less than usual and feel worried about it.

faq: Is it okay to eat the same few foods every day?

On hard days, yes. Repeating a handful of foods you can manage is a practical way to keep eating. Add variety again as your appetite returns, and talk to a dietitian if your options stay very limited.
Should I skip meals if I am not hungry?
Many people find small, regular meals easier than waiting for hunger. If you are unsure what is right for you, your care team can help you set a plan.
What if smells bother me while cooking?
Cook ahead on a better day, open a window, choose no-cook foods, or let food cool before eating. Cooler food usually smells less.

guides.title: Protein First: Easy Ways to Add Protein to Small Meals
guides.subtitle: Simple swaps and add-ins that fit more protein into a smaller plate, with estimated amounts for each.
intro: When you eat less, each bite has to do more. Starting a meal with its protein, and choosing ingredients that carry more protein per spoonful, makes it less likely that the protein is left on the plate when fullness arrives early. The rest of the meal still matters; this is only about the order.

This guide covers the protein-first habit, a table of easy add-ins with estimated amounts, and swaps that change a familiar recipe without changing how it feels to eat. How much protein you need is personal; your doctor or a registered dietitian can help you set a target.
takeaways: Eat the protein on your plate first, while your appetite is at its best.
Swap cream and oil for Greek yogurt, cottage cheese or white beans.
Add a protein to snacks, not just meals.
Protein amounts here are estimates; labels and portions vary.

p: Fullness can arrive early when your appetite is small. If you start with toast or pasta, you may be full before you reach the eggs or chicken. Eating the protein first is a simple habit that keeps it from being left behind.
It does not mean skipping everything else. Vegetables, fruit and grains still matter. It just changes the order on the plate.
These are rough estimates based on typical USDA reference values and package labels. Brands vary, so check the label when it matters.

sections.h: Swaps That Keep the Same Feel
p: You do not need new recipes to eat more protein. Small changes to familiar ones go a long way.
list: Cream in soups: Blend in a can of white beans, then stir in warmed Greek yogurt off the heat.
Oily dressings: Whisk Greek yogurt with lemon, a little olive oil and water until pourable.
Plain avocado toast: Mash the avocado with cottage cheese before spreading.
Pasta-heavy bowls: Use less pasta and more chicken, beans or edamame.
Pork sausage: Use lean turkey sausage and add egg whites to scrambles.

p: Small meals leave room for snacks between them. Pairing a snack with a protein makes it count for more.
list: Apple slices with a spoonful of peanut butter
Cottage cheese with berries
A hard-boiled egg and a few crackers
Greek yogurt with a little granola
Edamame with a pinch of salt

p: These recipes put the protein first. Values per serving are estimates.
list: One-Pan Shakshuka: Two eggs per plate with Greek yogurt, about 20 g protein.
Avocado Cottage Cheese Toast: About 20 g protein on one slice.
Lemon Chicken Orzo Soup: More chicken than pasta, about 27 g protein per bowl.
Grilled Chicken Avocado Salad: About 30 g protein per bowl.

faq: How much protein do I need?
It depends on your body, health and goals, so there is no single number that fits everyone. Your doctor or a registered dietitian can help you set a target that is right for you.
Are protein shakes a good idea?
They can be a convenient option for some people, especially on hard days. Check the label for protein and sugar, and ask your care team if you are unsure whether they fit your plan.
Why does Greek yogurt sometimes split in hot soup?
Its proteins tighten when they hit boiling, acidic liquid. Warm the yogurt with a ladle of soup first, stir it in off the heat and do not boil the soup afterwards.

guides.title: Small-Portion Meal Prep: Cook Once, Eat All Week
guides.subtitle: How to cook on a good day and portion food so a small, ready meal is always waiting in the fridge or freezer.
intro: Low-appetite days and low-energy days often arrive together. Meal prep in small portions means you do the cooking when you feel up to it, and on the harder days you only need to reheat a container.
This guide covers what to cook, how to portion it, what freezes well, and how to store and reheat food safely. Pick one or two recipes to start; you do not need to prep the whole week at once.
takeaways: Cook on a good day, portion small, and label everything.
Soups, sauces and burritos freeze well; cooked eggs and dressed salads do not.
Cool food quickly and refrigerate it within two hours.
Reheat until steaming, and keep sauces and dressings separate.

p: Some foods taste just as good on day three; others fall apart. These are good places to start.
list: Soups: Tomato, butternut squash and lemon chicken soups all keep for days. Leave out the pasta or yogurt if you plan to freeze them.
Sauces: Make shakshuka sauce ahead and poach fresh eggs in a single portion.
Breakfasts: Overnight oats in small jars keep for up to 4 days, and breakfast burritos freeze for months.
Grains and proteins: Cooked quinoa, edamame and chicken keep well for grain bowls and salads.

p: Portion food into containers right after cooking, in the size you can realistically finish. One cup is a good starting point for soups; a single small burrito or one 4 oz piece of fish is a good place to start.
Small containers also cool faster and reheat more evenly than one big pot.
list: Use 8 to 16 oz containers: Small glass jars and deli containers make portions easy to see.
Label everything: Write the recipe name and date on the lid.
Freeze flat: Lay bags of soup flat to freeze, then stack them like books.

p: These times match the storage notes on our recipes.

head: Food
Fridge
Freezer
Notes
rows: Stir in warmed yogurt when reheating
Cook a little fresh pasta when reheating

p: Food safety matters more when you cook ahead. These points follow general USDA food safety guidance.
list: Cool quickly: Refrigerate cooked food within 2 hours. Shallow containers cool faster.
Keep it cold: Keep your fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below and your freezer at 0°F (-18°C).
Use leftovers within 3 to 4 days: Freeze anything you will not eat in time.
Reheat thoroughly: Heat leftovers to 165°F (74°C), until steaming hot all the way through.
Thaw in the fridge: Move frozen portions to the fridge the night before.

p: If you have one good afternoon, this covers most of a week of small meals.
list: In the oven: Roast the squash for the butternut soup.
On the stove: Simmer the lemon chicken soup without the orzo.
In a bowl: Stir together three jars of overnight oats.
While things cook: Whisk a Greek yogurt dressing and cook a pot of quinoa.
To finish: Blend the squash soup, portion everything into small containers, label, and refrigerate or freeze.

faq: Do I need special containers?
No. Any airtight container works. Small glass jars and deli containers are inexpensive and make portion sizes easy to see.
Can I refreeze thawed soup?
Food thawed in the fridge can generally be refrozen, but the texture may suffer. Freezing in single portions means you only thaw what you need.
How do I keep prepped meals from getting boring?
Prep two or three recipes rather than one, and vary the toppings: a spoonful of yogurt, fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon or a few toasted seeds.

guides.title: Small Smoothies with Protein
guides.subtitle: How to build a small, sippable smoothie with real protein in it, and how to keep it from tasting like a chalky shake.
intro: On days when chewing feels like work, a smoothie can be the easiest way to get something useful in. The catch is that many smoothies are mostly fruit and juice: sweet, big and low in protein.

This guide shows a simple formula for a smaller smoothie built around protein, with add-ins and their estimated protein, plus a few fixes for texture and taste. It is general cooking education, not medical or nutrition advice.
takeaways: Start with a protein base: Greek yogurt, milk, soy milk or cottage cheese.
Use frozen fruit instead of ice so the smoothie stays thick, not watery.
A 1-cup smoothie you finish counts for more than a big one you abandon.
Sip slowly; you can keep half in the fridge for later.

p: Think of a smoothie as three parts: a protein base, a little fruit for flavor, and a liquid to get the blender moving. Everything else is optional.
list: Protein base: 1/2 to 3/4 cup plain Greek yogurt or 1/2 cup cottage cheese.
Fruit: 1/2 to 3/4 cup frozen berries, banana or mango.
Liquid: 1/2 cup milk, soy milk or ultra-filtered milk, plus more to thin.
Optional extras: A spoonful of peanut butter, oats, chia seeds or a little honey.

p: These are rough estimates based on typical USDA reference values and package labels. Brands vary a lot, especially protein powders and ultra-filtered milks, so check the label.
A smoothie that tastes chalky or separates in the glass is hard to finish. A few small changes help.
list: Too thin: Add more frozen fruit or a spoonful of yogurt, not ice.
Too thick: Add milk a tablespoon at a time.
Chalky from powder: Use less powder and more Greek yogurt, or blend the powder with the liquid first.
Cottage cheese texture: Blend it alone with the milk until completely smooth before adding fruit.
Too sweet: Skip juice and honey; let ripe banana or berries do the work.

p: You do not need a giant glass. Pour a 1-cup serving, refrigerate the rest in a sealed jar, and shake it before drinking later the same day. Smoothies with yogurt are best within 24 hours.
Each of these uses Greek yogurt as the protein base. Values per serving are estimates.
list: Strawberry Greek Yogurt Smoothie: About 16 g protein per glass.
Banana Vanilla Protein Smoothie: About 16 g protein per glass.
Mixed Berry Protein Smoothie: About 16 g protein per glass.

faq: Do I need protein powder?
No. Greek yogurt, cottage cheese and milk can carry a smoothie on their own. Powder is optional; if you use it, check the label for protein and added sugar.
Can I make smoothies ahead?
Yes, for the same day. Keep them sealed in the fridge and shake well. You can also freeze the fruit and yogurt portions in bags and blend with milk when you want one.
Can a smoothie stand in for a meal?
A smoothie is one easy option on harder days, not a replacement for varied meals. If you rely on them often, ask your care team or a registered dietitian whether your overall intake meets your needs.

guides.title: Eating Out with a Small Appetite
guides.subtitle: How to order, share and pack up at restaurants when a full entree is more than you can eat.
intro: Restaurant portions are often built for big appetites. When yours is smaller, a night out can feel like a choice between leaving most of your plate or eating more than feels comfortable.
There is a middle path. This guide covers how to read a menu for protein, how to order smaller without making a fuss, and how to turn leftovers into tomorrow's small plate.
takeaways: Look for the protein on the menu first, then build around it.
Appetizers, half portions and sides are often the right size.
Ask for a to-go box when the food arrives, not at the end.
Go easy on bread baskets and drinks before the meal arrives.

p: Scan for the dish where protein is the main event: grilled fish, chicken, eggs, beans, tofu or lean meat. Dishes built mostly on pasta, fries or bread can fill you up before you get much protein.
list: Good bets: Grilled fish or chicken, shrimp skewers, egg dishes, chili, lentil or bean soups, poke or rice bowls with extra protein.
Ask for swaps: Extra vegetables or a side salad instead of fries is a common, easy request.
Sauces on the side: Rich sauces add fullness quickly; on the side, you control how much you use.

p: Most restaurants are happy to help, and you do not need to explain why.
list: Order an appetizer as your meal: Shrimp cocktail, chicken skewers or a cup of soup is often the right size.
Ask about half or lunch portions: Many places offer them even at dinner if you ask.
Share an entree: Split one main and add a side or soup each.
Build from sides: A protein side plus a vegetable side makes an easy small plate.

p: A few habits make it easier to eat comfortably and enjoy the company.
list: Box it early: Ask for a to-go container when the food arrives and set aside half right away.
Protein first: Start with the protein on your plate while your appetite is at its best.
Pace yourself: Put your fork down between bites and stop when you are comfortably satisfied.
Sip between bites: Many people find that a lot of liquid with a meal makes them full sooner.

head: Cuisine
Smaller, protein-forward ideas
rows: Two eggs with fruit, a cup of chili, grilled chicken with a side salad
Chicken or shrimp tacos (order two), fajita protein with beans, chicken tortilla soup
Minestrone, grilled fish, a half portion of pasta with chicken
Miso soup, edamame, sashimi or a small poke bowl
Chicken or falafel plate with hummus, lentil soup, Greek salad with chicken
Egg drop or hot and sour soup, steamed chicken and vegetables, sharing a few dishes

p: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours (1 hour if it is very hot out) and eat them within 3 to 4 days. Reheat until steaming. Half a restaurant entree is often a ready-made small plate for the next day.

faq: Is it rude to ask for a smaller portion?
No. Asking for a half portion, an appetizer as a main or a to-go box is a normal request at most restaurants.
What about drinks?
Many people find carbonated drinks and large amounts of liquid make them feel full faster. If you drink alcohol, ask your care team whether it fits your situation.
What if nothing on the menu works?
A cup of soup and a side of vegetables, or a couple of appetizers, can work well. You can also eat a small protein snack before you go so you are not choosing on an empty stomach.

guides.title: High-Protein Grocery List for Small Appetites
guides.subtitle: A practical shopping list of protein-rich foods that keep well, need little cooking and fit into small meals.
intro: When your appetite is small, the easiest meals are the ones that are already in the kitchen. A well-stocked fridge and pantry means you can put together a protein-forward plate in minutes, even on a low-energy day.

This list is organized by where things live in a typical U.S. grocery store, with estimated protein amounts and ideas for using each item. Protein values are estimates based on USDA reference values and common labels.
takeaways: Keep a few no-cook proteins on hand: Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, eggs, canned fish.
Canned and frozen proteins are just as useful as fresh, and they last longer.
Buy smaller packages if you often throw food away.
Check labels: protein per serving varies by brand.

head: Item
Typical serving
Protein (estimate)
Use it for
rows: Toast, eggs, fruit bowls, mashed potatoes

list: Rotisserie chicken: Pull it the day you buy it and portion into small containers. About 25 g protein per 3 oz.
Lean ground turkey: For meatballs, taco bowls and stuffed peppers. About 22 g per cooked 3 oz.
White fish fillets: Cod or tilapia bake in under 15 minutes. About 19 to 20 g per 3 oz.
Salmon: About 22 g per cooked 3 oz; leftovers are good cold.
Shrimp (frozen, peeled): Cooks in minutes. About 20 g per 3 oz.
Canned tuna or salmon: About 17 to 20 g per drained 3 oz. Salads, wraps, crackers.
Canned beans and chickpeas: About 6 to 8 g per 1/2 cup. Soups, chili, blended into sauces.
Red lentils: Cook in about 20 minutes and blend into smooth soups.
Peanut butter: About 7 g per 2 tablespoons. Smoothies, toast, apple slices.
Bone broth: Some brands have 8 to 10 g per cup. Check the label.
Oats and chia seeds: Small protein boosts for breakfasts.
Shelled edamame: About 9 g per 1/2 cup. Snacks and grain bowls.
Frozen berries: For smoothies, parfaits and chia pudding.
Frozen fish fillets and shrimp: Thaw overnight in the fridge.
Frozen vegetables: Add to soups and stir-fries without any chopping.

p: If you are starting from an empty fridge, this covers several small meals and snacks for one person.
list: 1 large tub plain Greek yogurt
1 tub cottage cheese
1 dozen eggs
1 rotisserie chicken
2 cans tuna or salmon
2 cans beans or chickpeas
1 bag frozen berries
1 bag frozen edamame
Bread, crackers or tortillas you like

faq: Is canned or frozen protein less healthy?
Not necessarily. Canned fish and beans and frozen seafood are convenient, keep well and are widely used. If you watch sodium, look for low-sodium cans or rinse beans before using.
How do I avoid wasting food?
Buy smaller containers, freeze portions of cooked chicken or soup right away, and plan two or three recipes that share ingredients.
How much protein should I buy for?
That depends on your needs. Your doctor or a registered dietitian can help you set a daily target; this list is about having easy options on hand.

guides.title: Soft Foods for Hard Days
guides.subtitle: Smooth, mild, easy-to-eat foods with some protein in them, for days when chewing and strong flavors feel like too much.
intro: Some days call for food that asks very little of you: no hard crusts, no strong smells, nothing that takes a lot of chewing. Soft foods can still carry protein if you choose and build them well.

This guide lists soft, mild options, ways to add protein without changing the texture, and recipes from the site that fit. It is general cooking education. If you have trouble swallowing or a medical texture plan, follow your care team's guidance.
takeaways: Soft does not have to mean low protein: eggs, yogurt, cottage cheese and blended beans are all soft.
Warm or cool food is often easier than hot food.
Blending, mashing and slow cooking turn many foods soft.
Keep portions small and eat slowly.

head: Food
Why it works
Protein (estimate)
rows: Congee or rice porridge with chicken
Chia or rice pudding made with milk and yogurt

sections.h: Add Protein Without Changing the Texture
list: Stir warmed Greek yogurt into soups off the heat.
Blend cottage cheese into mashed potatoes or scrambled eggs.
Use milk or ultra-filtered milk instead of water in oatmeal and porridge.
Blend white beans into creamy soups.
Beat an egg into hot broth for an egg drop soup.
Cook longer: Simmer grains and vegetables until very tender.
Blend or mash: Use a blender, immersion blender or potato masher.
Add moisture: A spoonful of broth, milk or sauce makes food easier to swallow.
Cut small: Dice or shred meat and fish finely.
Skip the crust: Remove tough skins and crusts.
Chicken Rice Congee: Warm, soft rice porridge with shredded chicken.
Cottage Cheese Mashed Potatoes: Smooth mash with extra protein.
Greek Yogurt Chia Pudding: Cool and spoonable, made ahead.
Protein Rice Pudding: Soft and gently sweet.
Ginger Egg Drop Soup: Light broth with soft ribbons of egg.

faq: Is it fine to eat only soft foods for a few days?
On hard days, many people do. If soft foods are all you can manage for more than a few days, or you have pain or trouble swallowing, talk to your doctor or care team.
How do I keep soft food from being boring?
Change the toppings and temperature: a swirl of yogurt, fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, cinnamon on sweet dishes. Rotate between warm and cool options.
Can I freeze soft foods?
Many soups, congee and mashed potatoes freeze well in small portions. Yogurt-based dishes are better made fresh.

guides.title: Freezer Basics: What Keeps and for How Long
guides.subtitle: How to freeze, label, thaw and reheat small portions safely, with a simple chart of what freezes well.
intro: A freezer full of small portions is one of the best tools for low-appetite and low-energy days. Cook once on a good day, and there is always a ready meal waiting.
This guide covers how to freeze food so it keeps its quality, a chart of what freezes well, and how to thaw and reheat safely. The safety points follow general USDA food safety guidance.
takeaways: Keep your freezer at 0°F (-18°C).
Food kept frozen at 0°F stays safe, but quality is best within a few months.
Freeze in small, labeled, flat portions.
Thaw in the fridge and reheat to 165°F (74°C).

list: Cool first: Let food cool, then refrigerate within 2 hours before freezing.
Portion small: 1-cup containers or bags match a small plate.
Leave room: Liquids expand; leave about 1/2 inch at the top.
Remove air: Press air out of bags to limit freezer burn.
Freeze flat: Lay bags flat on a tray, then stack once frozen.
Label everything: Name and date on every container.

p: Times below are for best quality, not safety. Food kept frozen at 0°F remains safe longer, but texture and flavor slowly fade.

head: Food
Best quality within
Notes
rows: Freeze without pasta or yogurt; add those when reheating
Add a splash of broth to keep it moist
Freeze in a single layer first

list: Yogurt-based sauces and dressings: They separate.
Hard-boiled eggs: The whites turn rubbery.
Salad greens and cucumber: They go limp and watery.
Fried foods: They lose their crunch.
Dishes with cream or soft cheese: They may turn grainy.
In the fridge: The safest method. Move portions the night before.
In cold water: Seal in a bag and change the water every 30 minutes; cook right away.
In the microwave: Use the defrost setting and cook immediately.
Never on the counter: Food can warm into the unsafe range.
Reheat to 165°F (74°C): Until steaming hot all the way through. Stir soups halfway.
Creamy Split Pea Soup
Turkey Meatballs in Tomato Sauce
Freezer-Friendly Breakfast Burritos
Chicken Minestrone (freeze without the pasta)
Turkish-Style Red Lentil Soup

faq: Can I refreeze thawed food?
Food thawed in the fridge can generally be refrozen, though quality may drop. Food thawed in cold water or the microwave should be cooked before refreezing.
Is freezer burn unsafe?
No. Freezer burn affects texture and flavor, not safety. Trim off dry spots or use the food in soups.
Do I need special containers?
No. Freezer bags and airtight containers both work. Small sizes make portioning easier.
